Alright. Nine of us, one million dollars, and not one of you has said a word. Fine — I'm a chemistry teacher, I can't resist a controlled experiment, so let's get some data before anybody votes.

Me? Arvin Vijay, high school chemistry teacher. Yes, I set off a fire alarm once. Sodium. Nobody was hurt, but I still got a very stern phone call from a principal, so let's all agree nobody touches the beakers.

Start talking. And please, one at a time — I have trouble following a committee.

Hey everyone. Sarah Chen — marine biologist. I'll be honest, I'm more used to watching tide pools than reading people, so I'm going to listen more than I talk this round. Whoever has the money, you're already calculating how quiet to be. That's fine. Just know the rest of us are watching how you answer simple questions, not just whether you accuse someone. Anyone want to start with where you're from and what you actually do? Not a speech. One or two sentences.

First round, none of us has much to go on. I’m Ben, an insurance claims adjuster, so I’m interested in how people explain a decision more than how confident they sound. If you had to name one person to watch this round, who would it be and why?

I know everyone will say the same, so the claim proves little, but I'd still like each of us to say it on the record. What will matter is how people behave: who deflects, who pushes a name too quickly, who goes quiet. Could we go around and each say where we stand and what our gut tells us? A random vote in round 1 most likely sends an innocent person home with nothing, so I'd rather we base it on something we've actually seen.

Alright folks, let's get this party started! Marcus here, coming to you from just outside Columbus, Ohio. I'm in commercial HVAC sales, got a wife and two awesome little girls at home, and I'm pumped to be here. Let's not sit around staring at each other—who else have we got in the room, and more importantly, who's already sweating holding onto that million?

Hi everyone, I’m Emily—a high school teacher, so I’m used to a room full of people insisting they didn’t do it. 😂 With no history to work from, I’d rather hear everyone before picking a name. What would make you suspicious enough to vote for someone today? For me, it’s pushing a target hard while dodging questions about your own reasoning.

Good evening, everyone. I'd rather not vote on instinct alone, so let's start with some observation. Nobody has spoken yet, and silence tells us something too. I'd like each of you to give one concrete detail about how you're approaching this game. I'll go first: I'm watching who asks questions and who only makes accusations. Those two habits usually come from different places.

Hello everyone. I'm Elena. I'm an archivist by trade, so I tend to watch and listen before I speak. I think our best approach is to share observations carefully and avoid rash accusations. I'll be paying attention to inconsistencies. Good luck to us all.

Hi everyone, I'm Maya. Hospital operations coordinator by trade, which basically means I spend my days triaging chaos, so this setup feels weirdly familiar. Before anyone starts throwing accusations around, I'd like to suggest we actually talk this out. My read from experience: when someone's holding something big, they either go very quiet or very loud. I'll go first with my read: honestly, nothing solid yet, it's round one and we're all just faces on a screen. But I'd rather we vote on actual behavior than gut feelings or random picks. Anyone else have early impressions?

Sarah, you gave us your job but conveniently skipped the hometown I asked for. What city and state are you from? Marcus, “just outside Columbus” is close to a hometown; give us the actual town so we can verify it later. Everyone else still owes me a hometown. I’m not calling anyone a liar yet—I’m looking for answers that stay consistent.

Facts, since Arvin asked: Sarah Chen, marine biologist, Vancouver. That's the whole biography I'm giving out today.

Elias — did you see the earlier messages, or were you writing before they came in?

He set the agenda, put everyone else in the reporting seat, and claimed the one chair nobody's checking: the examiner's. That's either a genuinely helpful teacher running a class exercise, or exactly where a smart money holder would want to sit. I'm not voting on that — it's an observation, not an accusation. What would make it more is seeing how he handles being watched back.

If resting heart rate is the tell, we can save everyone time and vote alphabetically. Emily, to your question: what would actually move my vote is a caught contradiction on a checkable detail, or a vote push that only ever points away from the person making it.

Closing the facts on me so they stop circulating: Sarah Chen, marine biologist, Vancouver, British Columbia. I don't hold the money. Jordan asked everyone to say it on the record, so there it is — it still isn't evidence.

Marcus, listening first isn't the same as hiding. I answered when a direct question was asked, and I'll keep doing that. I won't invent a target just to look busy.

Elias, the question is still open: did you see the earlier messages, or were you writing before they arrived? A yes or no is enough.

Arvin, your hometown is still missing from the roll call you started, and the claim that the holder must lie about name, job, or city doesn't hold — they can tell the truth on all three. I'm watching how you answer that, not voting on it.
